question:
Patient note:
A 45-year-old woman with morbid obesity complicated only by diet-controlled prediabetes arrived in the ambulatory triage bay late this afternoon because her left lower leg had “bulged out of nowhere” over the prior twenty-four hours after an otherwise uneventful workday at her desk job. Six weeks earlier she underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy under general anesthesia; the procedure lasted two hours, she ambulated the same evening on the surgical floor, and she was discharged on postoperative day 2 with instructions for progressive walking, which she has followed faithfully, averaging 6 000–7 000 steps daily on her fitness tracker. She drives, climbs stairs, and sleeps in her own bed without assistive devices, has not worn braces or casts, and denies limb weakness, numbness, or spinal complaints. Her only medications are daily chewable multivitamins, pantoprazole 40 mg for expected postoperative reflux, and acetaminophen 500 mg taken twice last week for incisional soreness. She takes no estrogen preparations, glucocorticoids, hemopoietic agents, or anticoagulants, and there is no personal or first-degree family history of venous or pulmonary thrombosis. She never smoked, drinks a single hard seltzer on weekend evenings, and denies illicit drug use. Yesterday morning she felt normal until lunchtime, when she noticed the elastic cuff of her left jogger pant pressing into the calf more than usual; by bedtime the posterior compartment looked fuller in the mirror but remained painless, so she assumed muscular strain. On awakening today the asymmetry was more obvious, her sneaker felt tight, and she observed a faint web of bluish lines on the medial calf whenever she stood, prompting this visit. She denies external trauma, insect bites, rash, ulceration, fever, chills, night sweats, erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, groin mass, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, palpitations, light-headedness, hematuria, or recent air or road travel exceeding two hours. On arrival—before receiving any analgesic, fluid, or antithrombotic intervention—she sat comfortably with the leg elevated on a pillow, speaking in full sentences. Vital signs were temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate 86 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. The healing 1-cm port-site scars on the upper abdomen were dry and nontender; abdomen was soft with normal bowel sounds. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops, and lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. Inspection of the lower extremities demonstrated symmetric thighs and ankles, but the mid-calf circumference differed notably: using a cloth tape positioned exactly 10 cm distal to the inferior pole of the patella, nursing staff measured 41.9 cm on the symptomatic side versus 37.8 cm contralaterally, a 4.1-cm discrepancy; 15 cm above the patella both limbs measured 55.2 cm, and ankle girths at the malleoli were 26.1 cm left versus 26.0 cm right. With the leg dependent for thirty seconds a network of straight, non-tortuous superficial veins became prominent over the posteromedial calf and collapsed promptly upon elevation; no similar pattern appeared on the right. The overlying skin was taut and glossy but maintained uniform pink coloration, felt neither warmer nor cooler than the opposite side, and gentle thumb pressure over the pretibial crest rebounded immediately without an impression. Palpation of the quadriceps, adductor canal, popliteal fossa, gastrocnemius belly, and Achilles tendon elicited only diffuse pressure with no focal soreness, cord, fluctuance, or crepitus. Passive ankle dorsiflexion, knee flexion-extension, and hip rotation were full and painless. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill to all toes was <2 s, sensation to light touch and proprioception remained intact, and motor strength graded 5/5 in both lower limbs. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was appreciable, and straight-leg-raise testing did not provoke radicular pain. Point-of-care laboratory studies drawn prior to any imaging or medication showed hemoglobin 13.1 g dL⁻¹, platelet count 244 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocyte count 6.3 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, serum creatinine 0.88 mg dL⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained before laboratory draws demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats min⁻¹ without ST-T abnormalities. Weight-bearing radiographs of the tibia and fibula ordered by her primary surgeon earlier today showed intact cortices and only soft-tissue prominence corresponding to the clinically observed swelling. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle tear, lymphedema, or systemic fluid overload was evident on examination to account for the abrupt unilateral calf enlargement accompanied by newly visible superficial venous channels in the setting of recent bariatric surgery, so comprehensive duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral vein to the infrapopliteal segments was requested on an expedited basis while the patient remains hemodynamically stable and untreated in observation, her leg elevated above heart level pending imaging results.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Wells DVT score to the untreated admission findings:
- Bed rest for ≥3 days or major surgery under anesthesia within 12 weeks: sleeve gastrectomy under general anesthesia 6 weeks earlier, +1 despite early ambulation.
- Calf swelling ≥3 cm greater than the other side: 41.9 − 37.8 = 4.1 cm, +1.
- Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: newly prominent, straight superficial veins on the affected calf, +1.
- Active cancer, paralysis/paresis or recent cast immobilization, localized deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, unilateral pitting edema, and previous DVT: each absent, 0 each.
- Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT: none identified, so no 2-point deduction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
